title: Open-plan office noise is stressful: multimodal stress detection in a simulated work environment
research_question: To compare the effects of a typical open plan office auditory environment to a quieter private office auditory environment on a range of objective and subjective measures of well-being and performance.

participants.description: Forty healthy subjects (34 female, 6 male) with an age range of 17-44 years (mean age 22.65 years, SD=6.15). Participants were undergraduates and post-graduate students with university-level English and normal vision and hearing.
participants.recruitment: Recruited predominantly from a psychology subject pool; undergraduate students participated in exchange for course credit points.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Simulated open plan office background high noise condition. Soundscape included people speaking, walking, printing papers, ringing telephones, and keyboard typing noises. Average sound pressure level was 59.1 dB (A).
Simulated private office low noise condition. Background noise from air-conditioning and computer fan noise. Average sound pressure level was 36.3 dB (A).

measures.instrument: Proof-reading task (number of correctly identified typographical errors)
SHIMMER™ 3 GSR+ optical pulse oximeter (beats per minute)
SHIMMER™ 3 GSR+ optical pulse oximeter (Root Mean Square of the Successive Differences (RMSSD) in milliseconds)
iMotions AFFECTIVA (percent of time disgust expression present)
iMotions AFFECTIVA (percent of time anger expression present)

mechanisms: Noise creates additional cognitive demands and requires the application of resources and compensatory effort to maintain attention to one's central task.

Coping with the demands of noise should increase arousal in the short term and deplete an employee's store of job resources over the longer term, leaving less available to sustain performance and threatening feelings of self-efficacy.
Noise distractions that threaten goal progress are likely to create negative emotions such as frustration.
Office noise being perceived as norm-violating behaviour by others (socio-moral disgust).
Increased cognitive load of maintaining focus under distraction would deplete resources and damage performance following longer exposure.
Irrelevant intelligible speech may reduce processing capacity for any task that requires processing of written or spoken verbal information by competing for the limited store of verbal memory.
Abrupt office sounds will capture central processing resources away from the task, leading to lapses in performance in tasks requiring focused attention.
implementation_implications: HR experts are well positioned to advocate in a data-driven way for mutual gains in the re-design of workspaces.
Organizations should reconsider the design of workspaces to optimize outcomes for both employers and employees.

Rethink the different functions of the office within the context of hybrid work to enhance the quality of the physical work environment to benefit human well-being and desired organizational outcomes.
HR practices around the physical work environment may help produce mutual gains.

Organizations may wish to reconsider the extent to which open plan settings are deployed, as well as the use of acoustic treatments, sound masking technologies, reduced density and increased use of walls or partitions.
Social interventions to limit extraneous noise, interruptions, and technological distractions may also be helpful.

Reducing density and raising the height of walls between co-worker cubicles might be wise to reduce transmission of airborne illnesses, with the additional benefit of providing more employee privacy and less visual distraction.
HR specialists should monitor physical and psychological stressors linked to the physical work environment.
HR practitioners are better placed to design and modify workplaces to minimise negative effects of noise and support both employee well-being and organizational performance.
limitations: The most significant limitation is the short period of noise exposure, which may account for the non-significant results on the cognitive performance task.
The modest results for facial emotion recognition probably also suffered from the short duration of the work periods.
The use of a single task and cognitive performance measure, while distraction effects may differ depending on the demands of the task.
The study could be replicated in different age groups as working memory performance and capability for switching attentional focus reduces as age increases.
The effects of interruptions can be neutral or even positive dependent on a number of factors including whether the interruption was welcome, timely, or relevant to an existing task.
Individual differences may also condition the extent to which environmental distractors are harmful to well-being and performance.
The study simulated the acoustical environment of an open plan office in the lab, which may limit ecological validity.

paper_metadata.title: Open-plan office noise is stressful: multimodal stress detection in a simulated work environment
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Open-plan office noise is stressful: multimodal stress detection in a simulated work environment
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractThe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-2019)-induced changes in the workplace present a timely opportunity for human resource management practitioners to consider and remediate the deleterious effects of noise, a commonly cited complaint of employees working in open-plan office (OPO) environments. While self-reports suggest that OPO noise is perceived as a stressor, there is little experimental research comprehensively investigating the effects of noise on employees in terms of their cognitive performance, physiological indicators of stress, and affect. Employing a simulated office setting, we compared the effects of a typical OPO auditory environment to a quieter private office auditory environment on a range of objective and subjective measures of well-being and performance. While OPO noise did not reduce immediate cognitive task performance compared to the quieter environment, it did reduce psychological well-being as evidenced by self-reports of mood, facial expressions of emotion, and physiological indicators of stress in the form of heartrate and skin conductivity. Our research highlights the importance of using a multimodal approach to assess the impact of workplace stressors such as noise. Such an approach will allow HR practitioners to make data-driven recommendations about the design and modification of workspaces to minimize negative effects and support employee well-being.

mechanism_chain.description: Open-plan office noise acts as a stressor, leading to increased cognitive load and physiological arousal, which in turn impairs cognitive performance.

instruments_used.name: Proofreading task
instruments_used.description: Task requiring participants to identify errors in text

instruments_used.name: Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
instruments_used.construct: Physiological stress / autonomic nervous system activity
instruments_used.description: Measured via ECG or wearable sensors

instruments_used.name: Skin Conductance Level (SCL)
instruments_used.construct: Physiological arousal / sympathetic nervous system activity
instruments_used.description: Measured via electrodes on the skin
